positions.commentary: The speaker states that GM became cheaper and they bought it at much lower prices than originally what a debtor had paid for it.
The speaker mentions Amazon in the context of a hypothetical scenario where they missed a 10x or 100x gain because they said no to the investment.

thesis: The episode argues that General Motors (GM) represents a successful investment opportunity where the speaker entered the position at a price significantly lower than the original acquisition cost, resulting in substantial gains. The speaker also reflects on the regret of missing out on massive gains in other companies like Amazon, using these examples to illustrate the importance of recognizing when an investment idea makes sense.

claims.claim: The speaker decided to take a position in General Motors after realizing there were reasons why an investment made sense, noting they still own the position and are up more than 120%.
claims.quote: And it dawned on me that there were a number of reasons why an investment in GM made all the sense in the world. And that led me to actually take a position in GM. And we still own that position. I don't have much to say about it, except that we're up, I don't know, more than 120% so far on that position.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Amazon in the context of a hypothetical scenario where they missed a 10x or 100x gain because they said no to the investment.
claims.quote: So if someone brings me Amazon or Apple and in my moment of brilliance, I say no, in 2007 or 2003, and then it's a 10x or 100x. And we missed that ride. And no one made that money.

claims.claim: The speaker cites GM as an example of a good investment idea, noting they bought it at a much lower price than Berkshire Hathaway originally paid after the company became cheaper.
claims.quote: GM is a good example of that. The first time that was visible that Berkshire had bought, it was, I don't know, May, May 14th or May 15th or so.
